paragraphs: A firm Union will be of the utmost importance to the peace and liberty of the States as a barrier against domestic faction and insurrection. No one can read the history of the petty republics of Greece and Italy without horror and disgust at the distractions that continually agitated them, and at the rapid succession of revolutions that kept them swinging perpetually between the extremes of tyranny and anarchy. If they show occasional calms, these serve only as a brief contrast to the furious storms that are to follow. If now and then intervals of happiness open before us, we look on them with a mixture of regret, because we reflect that the pleasing scenes before us are soon to be overwhelmed by the stormy waves of sedition and party rage. If momentary rays of glory break out from the gloom, they dazzle us with a brief and fleeting brilliance, but at the same time they warn us to lament that the vices of government should distort the direction and tarnish the luster of those bright talents and exalted gifts for which the favored lands that produced them have been so justly celebrated.

But it cannot be denied that the portraits sketched of republican government were too accurate copies of the originals from which they were taken. If it had proved impracticable to devise models of a more perfect structure, the enlightened friends of liberty would have been obliged to abandon the cause of that kind of government as indefensible. The science of politics, however, like most other sciences, has been greatly improved. The effectiveness of various principles is now well understood, principles that were either not known at all, or only imperfectly known, to the ancients. The regular distribution of power into distinct departments; the introduction of legislative balances and checks; the institution of courts composed of judges who hold their offices during good behavior; the representation of the people in the legislature by deputies of their own election: these are wholly new discoveries, or have made their principal progress toward perfection in modern times. They are means, and powerful means, by which the excellences of republican government may be retained and its imperfections lessened or avoided. To this list of circumstances that tend to improve popular systems of civil government I shall venture to add one more, however novel it may appear to some. It rests on a principle that has been made the foundation of an objection to the new Constitution. I mean the ENLARGEMENT of the ORBIT within which such systems are to revolve, whether by enlarging the dimensions of a single State or by consolidating several smaller States into one great Confederacy. The latter is what immediately concerns the subject at hand. It will, however, be useful to examine the principle as it applies to a single State, which I shall do in another place.

The usefulness of a Confederacy, both for suppressing faction and guarding the internal tranquillity of States and for increasing their external force and security, is in reality not a new idea. It has been put into practice in different countries and ages, and the most respected writers on politics have approved it. The opponents of the proposed plan have diligently cited and circulated Montesquieu's remarks on the need for a small territory in a republican government. But they seem not to have known the views that great man expressed in another part of his work, nor to have noticed the consequences of the principle to which they so readily subscribe.

When Montesquieu recommends a small extent for republics, the models he had in mind were far smaller than almost any one of these States. Virginia, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, New York, North Carolina and Georgia cannot possibly be compared with the models he reasoned from and to which his description applies. If we take his ideas on this point as the standard of truth, then, we are forced into a choice. We must either flee at once into the arms of monarchy, or break ourselves up into an infinity of little, jealous, clashing, tumultuous commonwealths, the wretched breeding grounds of unceasing discord and the miserable objects of universal pity or contempt. Some of the writers on the other side of the question seem to have seen the dilemma, and have even been bold enough to hint that dividing the larger States would be desirable. Such an infatuated policy, such a desperate expedient, might suit men who lack the qualifications to extend their influence beyond the narrow circles of personal intrigue, since it would multiply petty offices. But it could never promote the greatness or happiness of the people of America.

As I have already said, I leave the examination of the principle itself to another place. It is enough to remark here that, in the sense intended by the author who has been most emphatically quoted on this occasion, the principle would require only that the more considerable MEMBERS of the Union be reduced in SIZE. It would not argue against their all being included in one confederate government. And this is the true question, the one that concerns us at present.

Montesquieu's suggestions are so far from standing in opposition to a general Union of the States that he explicitly treats a confederate republic as the means of extending the sphere of popular government and of combining the advantages of monarchy with those of republicanism.

"It is very probable," (says he(1)) "that mankind would have been obliged at length to live constantly under the government of a single person, had they not contrived a kind of constitution that has all the internal advantages of a republican, together with the external force of a monarchical government. I mean a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC."

"This form of government is a convention by which several smaller STATES agree to become members of a larger ONE, which they intend to form. It is a kind of assemblage of societies that constitute a new one, capable of increasing, by means of new associations, till they arrive to such a degree of power as to be able to provide for the security of the united body."
"A republic of this kind, able to withstand an external force, may support itself without any internal corruptions. The form of this society prevents all manner of inconveniences."

"If a single member should attempt to usurp the supreme authority, he could not be supposed to have an equal authority and credit in all the confederate states. Were he to have too great influence over one, this would alarm the rest. Were he to subdue a part, that which would still remain free might oppose him with forces independent of those which he had usurped and overpower him before he could be settled in his usurpation."

"Should a popular insurrection happen in one of the confederate states the others are able to quell it. Should abuses creep into one part, they are reformed by those that remain sound. The state may be destroyed on one side, and not on the other; the confederacy may be dissolved, and the confederates preserve their sovereignty."

"As this government is composed of small republics, it enjoys the internal happiness of each; and with respect to its external situation, it is possessed, by means of the association, of all the advantages of large monarchies."

I have thought it proper to quote these interesting passages at length, because they contain a luminous summary of the principal arguments in favor of the Union and must effectively remove the false impressions that a misapplication of other parts of the work was calculated to create. They are also closely connected with the more immediate purpose of this paper, which is to show the tendency of the Union to repress domestic faction and insurrection.

Some have drawn a distinction, more subtle than accurate, between a CONFEDERACY and a CONSOLIDATION of the States. They say the essential mark of the first is that its authority is limited to the members in their collective capacities and does not reach the individuals who make them up. They contend that the national council should have nothing to do with any matter of internal administration. They have also insisted that exact equality of votes among the members is a leading feature of a confederate government. These positions are, in the main, arbitrary, and neither principle nor precedent supports them. It is true that governments of this kind have generally worked in the way that the distinction takes to be inherent in their nature. But most of them have had extensive exceptions to that practice, which show, as far as example can, that there is no absolute rule on the subject. And it will be clearly shown in the course of this inquiry that wherever the principle contended for has prevailed, it has caused incurable disorder and weakness in the government.

A CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC seems to be defined simply as "an assemblage of societies," that is, an association of two or more states into one state. How far the federal authority extends, how it is shaped and what it is for are mere matters of discretion. As long as the separate organization of the members is not abolished, and exists by constitutional necessity for local purposes, the result would still be, in fact and in theory, an association of states, or a confederacy. That holds even if the members were in perfect subordination to the general authority of the union. The proposed Constitution, so far from implying an abolition of the State governments, makes them constituent parts of the national sovereignty by giving them a direct representation in the Senate, and it leaves in their possession certain exclusive and very important portions of sovereign power. This fully corresponds, in every rational sense of the terms, with the idea of a federal government.

The Lycian confederacy consisted of twenty-three CITIES or republics. The largest had THREE votes in the COMMON COUNCIL, those of the middle class had TWO, and the smallest had ONE. The COMMON COUNCIL appointed all the judges and magistrates of the individual CITIES. This was certainly the most delicate kind of interference in their internal administration, for if anything seems to belong exclusively to local jurisdictions, it is the appointment of their own officers. Yet Montesquieu, speaking of this association, says: "Were I to give a model of an excellent Confederate Republic, it would be that of Lycia." So we see that the distinctions insisted upon were never in the mind of this enlightened jurist, and we shall conclude that they are the novel refinements of an erroneous theory.
1. "Spirit of Laws," vol. i., book ix., chap. i.
